senses.def: a small solid piece of a substance with regular sides, formed naturally
examples: Salt crystals formed on the rocks as the seawater dried.
Snowflakes are made of tiny ice crystals.

senses.def: high-quality clear glass used for fine glasses and decorations
examples: They received a set of crystal wine glasses as a wedding gift.

note: "Crystal clear" = completely clear or easy to understand: "Let me make this crystal clear."

senses.def: an action or event that signals someone to do something
examples: When the music stops, that's your cue to walk on stage.
She took her cue from the host and started eating.

senses.def: a long stick used to hit the ball in pool or billiards
examples: He chalked the end of his cue before taking the shot.

note: "Right on cue" = at exactly the expected moment. Don't confuse with British "queue" (line), which sounds the same.

senses.def: a small religious group with extreme beliefs, often controlled by one leader
examples: Her parents spent years trying to get her out of the cult.

senses.def: a way of life, idea, or person that has become extremely popular
examples: Some critics complain about the cult of celebrity on social media.

senses.def: very popular with a particular group of fans
examples: The movie flopped at first but later became a cult classic.
The band has a cult following in Japan.

senses.def: to prepare land and grow crops on it
examples: Farmers here have cultivated rice for centuries.
Only a small part of the land is suitable for cultivating.

senses.def: to try to develop a quality, skill, or relationship
examples: She has cultivated an image as a tough negotiator.
It's worth cultivating good relationships with your clients.

senses.def: connected with the customs, beliefs, and way of life of a society
examples: Moving abroad can be a big cultural shock.
The city has a rich cultural heritage.

senses.def: connected with art, music, theater, and literature
examples: The festival is the biggest cultural event of the year.

senses.def: the customs, beliefs, art, and way of life of a particular society or group
examples: Food is an important part of Turkish culture.
Children of immigrants often grow up between two cultures.

senses.def: the attitudes and behavior typical of an organization or group
examples: The company has a culture of working late every night.

senses.def: art, music, literature, and similar activities
examples: Paris is full of culture: museums, theaters, and galleries.

note: In Turkish, "kültürlü" (educated) is closer to "cultured" or "well-read" in English.

senses.def: a small container with a handle used for drinking, or the amount it holds
examples: Would you like a cup of coffee?
Add one cup of flour to the mixture.

senses.def: a large metal cup given as a prize, or the competition for it
examples: Brazil has won the World Cup five times.

note: "Not my cup of tea" = not something I like. In US recipes, a "cup" is a standard measure (about 240 ml).

senses.def: a piece of furniture or a space in a wall with doors and shelves, used for storing things
examples: The plates are in the cupboard above the sink.
We keep cleaning supplies in the cupboard under the stairs.

note: Pronounced /ˈkʌbərd/: the p is silent. Americans usually say "cabinet" in kitchens and "closet" for clothes.

senses.def: a medicine or treatment that makes an illness go away
examples: Scientists are still searching for a cure for Alzheimer's.
There is no cure for the common cold.

senses.def: something that solves a problem
examples: Lower taxes are not a cure for every economic problem.

senses.def: to make a person or animal healthy again, or to end an illness or problem
examples: The treatment cured her of the infection in two weeks.
Nothing will cure his habit of arriving late.

note: "Cure" means to fully heal; "treat" means to give medical care, which may or may not cure.

senses.def: a strong wish to know or learn about something
examples: Out of curiosity, I opened the box to see what was inside.
Children are full of natural curiosity about the world.

senses.def: an unusual and interesting object or person
examples: The old shop was full of curiosities from around the world.

note: "Curiosity killed the cat" warns that being too curious can get you into trouble.

senses.def: wanting to know or learn about something
examples: I'm curious to know how the story ends.
The kids were curious about the strange noise in the attic.

senses.def: strange and unusual
examples: There was a curious smell coming from the basement.

note: "Just curious" is a polite way to show you're asking out of interest, not suspicion.

senses.def: having curls or a curved shape
examples: She has long curly hair that she usually ties back.
The puppy has a short curly tail.

note: Opposite: straight hair. "Curly brackets" are { }.

senses.def: the system of money used in a particular country
examples: The euro is the official currency of 20 European countries.
You can exchange foreign currency at the airport.

senses.def: the state of being generally accepted or used
examples: The idea gained currency among economists in the 1980s.

note: "Gain currency" = become widely accepted (used for ideas and words).

senses.def: happening or existing now
examples: What's your current address?
The current situation is better than it was a year ago.

senses.def: a movement of water or air in a particular direction
examples: The current was too strong for the swimmers.
Warm ocean currents keep the coast mild in winter.

senses.def: a flow of electricity through a wire
examples: Turn off the current before you touch the wires.

note: Don't confuse with "currant" (a small dried fruit), which sounds the same.

senses.def: at the present time
examples: She's currently working on her second novel.
The museum is currently closed for renovation.

note: Trap for Turkish speakers: "actually" does NOT mean "currently" (aktüel). Use "currently" for "şu anda".

senses.def: the subjects included in a course of study or taught in a school
examples: Coding has been added to the elementary school curriculum.
The university is reviewing its curriculum for first-year students.

note: Plural: curricula or curriculums. A CV (curriculum vitae) is usually called a "résumé" in the US.

senses.def: a piece of cloth hung to cover a window or divide a space
examples: Could you close the curtains? The sun is in my eyes.
She pulled back the shower curtain.

senses.def: the large cloth in front of a theater stage
examples: The audience clapped as the curtain came down.

note: Americans also say "drapes" for heavy curtains. "Curtain call" = when actors come back to bow.

senses.def: a line or surface that bends smoothly, or a bend in a road
examples: Slow down: there's a sharp curve ahead.
The graph shows a steady upward curve in sales.

senses.def: to bend or move in a smooth round line
examples: The path curves gently down to the beach.
The ball curved into the top corner of the net.

note: "A steep learning curve" = something that takes a lot of effort to learn quickly.

senses.def: having a round, bent shape rather than a straight one
examples: The bridge has a beautiful curved design.
A parrot uses its strong curved beak to crack nuts.

note: Opposite: straight.

senses.def: the legal right to care for a child, especially after parents separate
examples: After the divorce, the mother was given custody of the children.
They share joint custody of their son.

senses.def: the state of being held by the police, usually before a trial
examples: The suspect is now in police custody.
Two men were taken into custody after the robbery.

note: In the US, a "custodian" is also a building janitor.

senses.def: a traditional way of doing something in a society or group
examples: In Japan, it is the custom to take off your shoes indoors.
Giving gifts at New Year is an old local custom.

senses.def: made specially for a particular customer
examples: They ordered custom furniture for the new house.

note: "Customs" (plural) is the place at a border where bags are checked: "go through customs".

senses.def: a person or organization that buys goods or services from a business
examples: The store gives regular customers a 10% discount.
Call customer service if your package doesn't arrive.

note: "Client" is used for professional services (lawyers, agencies); "customer" for shops and companies.

senses.def: to divide, open, or shape something with a knife, scissors, or other sharp tool
examples: Cut the onions into small pieces.
I cut my finger while opening the package.

senses.def: to reduce the amount, size, or number of something
examples: The company plans to cut 2,000 jobs this year.
Try to cut down on sugar.

senses.def: a wound made by something sharp
examples: He had a deep cut on his hand from the broken glass.

senses.def: a reduction in amount or size
examples: Teachers protested against the budget cuts.

note: Irregular verb: cut – cut – cut. "Cut it out!" (informal) = stop doing that.

senses.def: pretty and attractive, especially in a small or childlike way
examples: Look at that cute little puppy!
The baby looks so cute in that hat.

senses.def: (informal) sexually attractive
examples: She thinks the new guy at work is really cute.

senses.def: trying too hard to be clever, in an annoying way
examples: Don't get cute with me; just answer the question.

senses.def: (British) an article or picture cut from a newspaper or magazine
examples: Her mother kept a folder of newspaper cuttings about her career.

senses.def: a piece cut from a plant to grow a new plant
examples: I took a cutting from my neighbor's rose bush and planted it.

senses.def: unkind and meant to hurt someone's feelings, or (of wind) very cold
examples: He made a cutting remark about her weight.
A cutting wind blew off the lake.

note: Americans say "newspaper clipping" rather than "cutting". "Cutting-edge" = the most advanced.

senses.def: a series of events that repeat in the same order
examples: The program aims to break the cycle of poverty.
The washing machine takes an hour to finish one cycle.

senses.def: a bicycle or motorcycle
examples: The city has built new cycle lanes downtown.

senses.def: to ride a bicycle
examples: She cycles to work every day, even in winter.

note: In everyday American English, people usually say "bike" and "ride a bike" rather than "cycle".

senses.tr: kinik, şüpheci, her şeye kötü gözle bakan
senses.def: believing that people usually act only for selfish reasons, not honest or good ones
examples: Many voters have become cynical about politicians' promises.
Years of working in sales made him cynical.

senses.def: caring only about your own advantage, without regard for others
examples: The ad campaign was a cynical attempt to make money from a tragedy.

senses.def: (informal) father
examples: My dad taught me how to ride a bike.
Dad, can you pick me up after practice?

note: Write "Dad" with a capital letter when used as a name. A "dad joke" is a corny, predictable joke.

senses.def: happening, done, or produced every day
examples: Exercise should be part of your daily routine.
The museum gets about 5,000 daily visitors.

senses.def: every day
examples: Take the medicine twice daily with food.
The newspaper is published daily.

senses.def: a newspaper published every day
examples: The story was on the front page of every national daily.

senses.def: milk, cheese, butter, and other foods made from milk
examples: She's allergic to dairy, so she drinks oat milk.
Try to eat less meat and dairy.

senses.def: made from milk, or connected with producing milk
examples: Dairy products are a good source of calcium.
He grew up on a dairy farm in Wisconsin.

note: Don't confuse "dairy" /ˈderi/ with "diary" /ˈdaɪəri/ (a daily journal).

senses.def: a wall built across a river to hold back water, often to make a lake or produce electricity
examples: The Hoover Dam supplies electricity to millions of people.
Heavy rain caused the old dam to burst.

senses.def: to build a dam across a river
examples: The river was dammed in the 1960s to create a reservoir.

note: Don't confuse with "damn" (a swear word), which sounds the same.

senses.def: physical harm that makes something less useful, valuable, or attractive
examples: The storm caused serious damage to homes along the coast.
Smoking can cause permanent damage to your lungs.

senses.def: to harm something physically, or to have a bad effect on something
examples: Several cars were damaged in the flood.
The scandal damaged the company's reputation.

senses.def: money that a court orders someone to pay for causing harm or loss
examples: She was awarded $2 million in damages.

note: "Damage" (harm) is uncountable: "a lot of damage", not "damages". "Damages" means money paid by court order.

senses.def: causing harm or having a bad effect
examples: The leaked emails were deeply damaging to her campaign.
Too much sun can be damaging to your skin.

senses.def: to move your body to music
examples: We danced all night at their wedding.
Do you want to dance?

senses.def: a set of movements done to music, or an occasion when people dance
examples: The tango is a dance from Argentina.
Are you going to the school dance on Friday?

senses.def: a person who dances, especially as a job
examples: She trained as a ballet dancer in New York.
I'm not a very good dancer, so I'll just watch.

note: In Turkish "dansöz" means a belly dancer; in English that is "belly dancer". "Dancer" is general.

senses.def: the activity of moving your body to music
examples: Let's go dancing on Saturday night.
She takes dancing lessons twice a week.

senses.def: the possibility of being hurt, killed, or harmed
examples: The sign warned of danger from falling rocks.
Doctors say the patient is now out of danger.

senses.def: something or someone that may cause harm, or the risk that something bad will happen
examples: Icy roads are a real danger to drivers.
There's a danger that prices will rise again.

senses.def: likely to cause injury, harm, or damage
examples: It's dangerous to text while driving.
Police say the escaped prisoner is armed and dangerous.

senses.def: to be brave enough to do something
examples: Nobody dared to tell the boss about the mistake.
I didn't dare look down from the top of the tower.

senses.tr: (birine bir şey yapması için) meydan okumak
senses.def: to challenge someone to do something dangerous or difficult
examples: His friends dared him to jump into the freezing lake.

senses.def: a challenge to do something risky
examples: She ate the hot pepper on a dare.

note: "How dare you!" expresses anger. "Don't you dare!" is a strong warning. "Dare" can be followed by an infinitive with or without "to".

senses.def: with little or no light
examples: It gets dark around five o'clock in winter.
The hallway was too dark to see anything.

senses.def: close to black in color, or (of hair, eyes, skin) brown or black
examples: He wore a dark blue suit to the interview.
She has dark hair and green eyes.

senses.def: sad, unpleasant, or evil
examples: The film has a much darker ending than the book.

senses.def: the lack of light, especially at night
examples: Many kids are afraid of the dark.
Be home before dark.

note: "Keep someone in the dark" = not tell them what is happening.

senses.def: the state of having no light
examples: The power went out and the whole street was plunged into darkness.
We drove home in darkness after the concert.

senses.def: evil or sadness
examples: The novel explores the darkness inside ordinary people.

note: "Under cover of darkness" = hidden by the night.

senses.def: facts or information, especially when collected and studied to learn something or make decisions
examples: The data shows a sharp rise in housing prices.
Researchers collected data from over 10,000 patients.

senses.def: information stored or used by a computer, or mobile internet usage
examples: I've used up all my data for this month.
Hackers stole personal data from millions of users.

note: In American English, "data" is usually treated as uncountable: "the data is". "The data are" is more formal/academic.

senses.def: an organized collection of information stored on a computer that can be searched easily
examples: The police checked his fingerprints against a national database.
All customer orders are stored in a central database.

senses.def: a particular day of the month or year
examples: What's the date today?
Please write the date at the top of the form.

senses.def: a romantic meeting, or a person you go out with romantically
examples: They went on their first date to a little Italian restaurant.
Who's your date for the wedding?

senses.def: to have a romantic relationship with someone
examples: They dated for three years before getting married.

senses.tr: tarih atmak; (yaşını) tarihlendirmek; (from ile) -den kalma olmak
senses.def: to write the date on something, or to say or show how old something is
examples: The letter was dated May 3, 1945.
This church dates from the 12th century.

note: US date format is month/day/year: 3/5/2026 = March 5. "Date" is also the sweet fruit (hurma).

senses.def: a person's female child
examples: They have two sons and a daughter.
My daughter just started kindergarten.

note: The "gh" is silent: /ˈdɔːtər/. A "daughter-in-law" is your son's wife (gelin).

senses.def: the time of day when light first appears
examples: We left at dawn to avoid the traffic.
The fishermen work from dawn until dusk.

senses.def: the beginning of a period of time or of something new
examples: The invention of the printing press marked the dawn of a new age.

senses.def: if something dawns on you, you realize it for the first time
examples: It suddenly dawned on me that I had left my passport at home.

note: "It dawned on me" = I suddenly realized. Opposite of dawn: dusk.

senses.def: a period of 24 hours
examples: The store is open seven days a week.
I'll call you in a few days.

senses.def: the time when it is light outside, between sunrise and sunset
examples: He works during the day and studies at night.

senses.def: a particular period in history or in someone's life
examples: In my grandfather's day, nobody had a phone at home.
These days, almost everyone works online.

note: "Call it a day" = stop working for now. "The other day" = a few days ago.

senses.def: no longer alive
examples: Two people were found dead in the burned house.
My grandparents have been dead for years.

senses.def: not working because of no power, or very quiet with no activity
examples: My phone is dead; can I borrow your charger?
This town is completely dead after 9 p.m.

senses.def: (informal) completely or exactly
examples: I'm dead serious about quitting my job.
The hotel is dead ahead, at the end of the street.

note: "Dead" is the adjective, "die" the verb, "death" the noun. Don't say "He is died"; say "He is dead" or "He died".

senses.def: a time or date by which something must be finished
examples: The deadline for applications is March 1.
I'm working late tonight to meet a deadline.

senses.def: causing or likely to cause death
examples: It was the deadliest earthquake in the country's history.
Some mushrooms in these woods are deadly.

senses.def: extremely serious or accurate, or (informal) very boring
examples: She's a deadly accurate shooter.
He said it in deadly earnest.

note: "Deadly" is an adjective despite the -ly ending. "Fatal" describes something that actually killed; "deadly" can mean able to kill.

senses.def: an agreement, especially in business, about buying, selling, or doing something
examples: The two companies signed a $3 billion deal.
I got a great deal on this laptop.

senses.def: a large amount
examples: She spends a great deal of time helping others.

senses.tr: (with ile) ilgilenmek, başa çıkmak, ele almak
senses.def: to take action to solve a problem or handle a situation or person
examples: The manager will deal with your complaint.
I can't deal with this right now.

senses.def: to give out playing cards, or to buy and sell drugs or goods
examples: It's your turn to deal the cards.
He was arrested for dealing drugs.

note: Irregular verb: deal – dealt – dealt. "No big deal" = not important.

senses.def: a person or business that buys and sells a particular product
examples: We bought the car from a dealer in New Jersey.
She's an art dealer with a gallery in Chicago.

senses.def: a person who sells illegal drugs
examples: Police arrested three drug dealers near the park.

senses.def: used at the start of a letter or email before the person's name
examples: Dear Ms. Lopez, thank you for your application.
She started the email with "Dear team".

senses.def: loved by someone, or very important to them
examples: She's a dear friend of mine.
This house is very dear to me.

senses.def: used to show surprise, worry, or disappointment
examples: Oh dear, I've forgotten my wallet again.
Dear me, look at the time!

senses.def: used to speak to someone you love or are being kind to
examples: Thank you, dear, that's very kind.

note: "Pay dearly" = suffer a lot because of a mistake. In British English, "dear" can mean expensive.

senses.def: the end of someone's life, or the fact of dying
examples: The cause of death is still unknown.
His father's death hit him very hard.

senses.def: the end of something
examples: Online shopping has meant the death of many small bookstores.

note: "To death" adds emphasis: bored to death, scared to death. "Death toll" = number of people killed.

senses.def: a formal discussion in which people with different opinions argue, often followed by a vote
examples: The two candidates will face each other in a televised debate.
There is a heated debate over gun control.

senses.def: to discuss something formally, or to think carefully before deciding
examples: Congress is debating a new immigration bill.
I debated whether to call her or not.

note: "Debate" is used without "about" as a verb: "debate the issue", not "debate about the issue".

senses.def: broken pieces of something left after it has been destroyed
examples: Rescue workers searched through the debris after the earthquake.
The storm left debris scattered across the highway.

note: Pronounced /dəˈbriː/: the s is silent. Uncountable: "a lot of debris".

senses.def: money that someone owes, or the state of owing money
examples: Many students graduate with huge debts.
He's been in debt since he lost his job.

senses.def: a feeling that you should be grateful to someone for their help
examples: I owe you a debt of gratitude for all your support.

note: The b is silent: /det/. "In debt" = owing money.

senses.def: a system for sending messages between computers, or a message sent this way
examples: I got an email from my landlord about the rent increase.
Please send your application by email before Friday.

senses.def: to send a message or a file to someone by email
examples: Can you email me the slides after the meeting?
She emailed the whole team to cancel the call.

note: Also spelled "e-mail". In speech, Americans often just say "I'll send it to you" or "I'll shoot you an email" (informal).

senses.tr: (yeni ve zor bir işe) girişmek, başlamak
senses.def: to start something new, important, or difficult (used with on or upon)
examples: After college, she embarked on a career in journalism.
The city is embarking on an ambitious plan to rebuild its subway.

senses.def: to get onto a ship or plane at the start of a journey
examples: Passengers began to embark at the port just after dawn.

note: The "start" sense is far more common and always takes "on/upon": embark on a new venture.

senses.def: feeling uncomfortable or ashamed, especially because of what other people think of you
examples: I was so embarrassed when I called my teacher "Mom" in class.
He felt embarrassed about forgetting her name.

note: Spelled with double r and double s. Embarrassed = how you feel; embarrassing = the situation that causes it. Not the same as "ashamed" (guilt).

senses.def: making you feel uncomfortable, silly, or ashamed in front of others
examples: It was embarrassing to trip on stage in front of the whole school.
The leaked emails were deeply embarrassing for the company.

note: -ing describes the cause (an embarrassing question); -ed describes the person's feeling (I was embarrassed).

senses.def: the uncomfortable feeling you have when you are ashamed or feel silly in front of others
examples: His face turned red with embarrassment.
To my embarrassment, my phone rang during the funeral.

senses.def: a person or thing that makes others feel ashamed
examples: The failed launch was a major embarrassment for the government.

senses.def: the official building or group of diplomats that represents a country in a foreign capital
examples: She went to the embassy to apply for a student visa.
Protesters gathered outside the US embassy in the capital.

note: An embassy is in the capital; a consulate (konsolosluk) is a smaller office in other cities.

senses.def: to fix something firmly inside a surrounding material or object
examples: A piece of glass was embedded in his foot.
The fossils are embedded in layers of rock.

senses.tr: (fikir, kültür vb.) kök salmak, yerleşmek; (web) yerleştirmek
senses.def: to make an idea or habit a deep part of something; to put a video, link, etc. into a web page
examples: Racism is deeply embedded in some institutions.
You can embed the video directly on your blog.

note: Very often used in the passive: "be embedded in". The doubled d appears in embedded, embedding.

senses.tr: somutlaştırmak, temsil etmek, -in vücut bulmuş hali olmak
senses.def: to express or represent an idea or quality clearly and completely
examples: For many fans, the team captain embodies the spirit of the club.
The new constitution embodies the values of freedom and equality.

note: "The embodiment of" is common: she is the embodiment of kindness (iyiliğin vücut bulmuş hali).

senses.def: to put your arms around someone to show love or friendship
examples: The two brothers embraced at the airport after ten years apart.

senses.def: to accept a new idea, belief, or change willingly and with enthusiasm
examples: Many older workers have embraced remote work.
The town has embraced tourism as a source of income.

senses.def: the act of holding someone close in your arms
examples: She greeted her grandson with a warm embrace.

note: In everyday speech "hug" is the usual word for the physical act; "embrace" sounds more formal or literary.

senses.def: to come out from a hidden or dark place and become visible
examples: A deer emerged from the trees and crossed the road.
The sun emerged from behind the clouds.

senses.def: to become known, especially after being hidden or unclear
examples: It later emerged that the mayor had known about the problem.
New details have emerged about the crash.

senses.def: to start to exist or become important; to come out of a difficult situation
examples: Several new tech hubs have emerged in the Midwest.
The company emerged from bankruptcy stronger than before.

note: "Emerging markets" (gelişmekte olan piyasalar) is a very frequent economics phrase.

senses.def: the process of appearing, starting to exist, or becoming known or important
examples: The emergence of smartphones changed how people read the news.
Scientists are tracking the emergence of a new virus strain.

note: Do not confuse with "emergency" (acil durum).

senses.def: a sudden, serious, dangerous situation that needs action immediately
examples: In an emergency, call 911.
The plane made an emergency landing after one engine failed.

note: American: "emergency room (ER)" = acil servis. The British say "A&E". In the US you dial 911.

senses.def: the release of gas, heat, light, etc. into the air, or an amount that is released
examples: The new law aims to cut carbon emissions by half by 2035.
Cars must pass an emissions test every two years.

note: Usually plural (emissions) when talking about pollution.

senses.def: a strong feeling such as love, fear, or anger, or feelings in general as opposed to reason
examples: She tried hard to hide her emotions during the interview.
His voice was full of emotion as he thanked his parents.

senses.def: connected with people's feelings
examples: Children need emotional support as well as food and shelter.
Losing a job can take a huge emotional toll.

senses.def: showing strong feelings, often by crying; causing strong feelings
examples: He got very emotional during his farewell speech.
Immigration remains an emotional issue for many voters.

senses.def: in a way that is connected with feelings, or in a way that shows strong feeling
examples: Caring for a sick parent can be emotionally exhausting.
She spoke emotionally about her years in the refugee camp.

senses.def: special importance or attention given to something
examples: The school puts a strong emphasis on reading and writing.
There is now more emphasis on prevention than treatment.

senses.def: extra force given to a word or syllable when speaking
examples: She said "never" with heavy emphasis.

note: Plural: emphases. Use "emphasis on" (not "to"): The emphasis is on quality.

senses.def: to show or say that something is especially important
examples: The doctor emphasized the need for regular exercise.
I want to emphasize that nobody will lose their job.

note: No preposition: emphasize something (NOT emphasize on something). British spelling: emphasise.

senses.def: a group of countries controlled by one ruler or government
examples: The Ottoman Empire lasted for more than six centuries.
At its height, the Roman Empire stretched from Britain to Egypt.

senses.def: a large group of businesses controlled by one person or company
examples: He built a media empire from a single local newspaper.

senses.def: based on observation, experiments, or experience rather than theory
examples: There is little empirical evidence that the diet works.
The study offers an empirical analysis of wage data from 40 countries.

note: Academic word. Opposite: theoretical.

senses.def: to pay someone to work for you
examples: The factory employs about 300 people from the town.
She is employed as a nurse at the local hospital.

senses.def: to use a particular method, skill, or tool (formal)
examples: The researchers employed a range of techniques to collect data.

note: In everyday speech, "hire" is more common for taking on a new worker.

senses.def: a person who is paid to work for a company or another person
examples: The company gave every employee a bonus at the end of the year.
Part-time employees are not eligible for health insurance.

note: Employee = the person who works; employer = the person or company that pays. Stress is on the last syllable for many speakers.

senses.def: a person or organization that pays people to work for them
examples: The hospital is the largest employer in the county.
Ask your employer whether they offer a retirement plan.

senses.def: paid work, or the state of having a paid job
examples: Many graduates struggle to find employment in their field.
Employment in manufacturing has fallen sharply since the 1980s.

senses.def: the use of something for a particular purpose (formal)
examples: The employment of new teaching methods improved test scores.

senses.def: to give someone the power, confidence, or legal right to do something
examples: The program aims to empower women to start their own businesses.
The new law empowers police to stop and search vehicles.

senses.def: with nobody or nothing inside
examples: The streets were empty at three in the morning.
Don't put the empty milk carton back in the fridge.

senses.def: having no real meaning, value, or purpose
examples: Voters are tired of empty promises.
After the divorce, his life felt empty.

senses.def: to remove everything from a container or place, or to become empty
examples: Could you empty the dishwasher before you go?
The stadium emptied quickly after the final whistle.

note: "On an empty stomach" = aç karnına. "Vacant" is used for seats, rooms, and jobs.

senses.def: to make it possible for someone to do something or for something to happen
examples: The scholarship enabled her to study abroad.
New software enables doctors to share records instantly.

senses.def: to turn on a feature or function on a computer or device
examples: You need to enable cookies to use this website.

note: Pattern: enable + object + to-infinitive (enable us to save time), NOT enable to do.

senses.def: to make a proposal into law
examples: Congress enacted the law with support from both parties.
Several states have enacted stricter gun laws.

senses.def: to perform a story or scene, for example in a play (formal)
examples: The students enacted a scene from the trial.

note: Formal, used in law and politics.

senses.def: to include a wide range of things or ideas
examples: The course encompasses both ancient and modern history.
Her job encompasses everything from hiring to payroll.

senses.def: to surround an area completely
examples: The national park encompasses three lakes and a large forest.

senses.def: to experience something, especially a problem or something difficult
examples: We encountered heavy traffic on the way to the airport.
Please call us if you encounter any problems with the app.

senses.def: to meet someone or see something, especially unexpectedly
examples: It was the strangest animal she had ever encountered.

senses.def: a meeting, often a sudden or unexpected one, or a brief experience of something
examples: He described his close encounter with a bear in Alaska.
A chance encounter on a train changed her life.

note: Formal for "run into" or "come across". Pattern: encounter something (no preposition).

senses.def: to give someone support, confidence, or hope so they will do something
examples: My parents always encouraged me to follow my dreams.
Teachers should encourage students to ask questions.

senses.def: to make something more likely to happen or develop
examples: Low interest rates encourage people to borrow more.
The city wants to encourage the use of public transit.

senses.def: words or actions that give someone confidence or hope to do something
examples: With her coach's encouragement, she entered the marathon.
Shy children need a lot of encouragement to speak in class.

senses.def: giving you hope or confidence that something will succeed
examples: The early results of the trial are very encouraging.
It's encouraging to see so many young people voting.

senses.def: the final part of a period of time, event, activity, or story
examples: We're moving to Denver at the end of the month.
I didn't understand the end of the movie.

senses.def: the furthest point or part of something long
examples: Our house is at the end of the street.

senses.tr: bitmek, sona ermek; bitirmek, sona erdirmek
senses.def: to finish, or to make something finish
examples: The meeting ended with a vote.
Both sides want to end the war.

note: "In the end" = eventually (sonunda); "at the end (of)" = at the final point of. "End up" = to finally be in a situation.

senses.def: a serious attempt to do something new or difficult (formal)
examples: Space exploration is one of humanity's greatest endeavors.
We wish you success in all your future endeavors.

senses.def: to try very hard to do something (formal)
examples: We will endeavor to answer every email within 24 hours.

note: British spelling: endeavour. Formal; in speech, use "try" or "effort".

senses.def: the last part of a story, movie, or event
examples: I love books with a happy ending.
The show's ending left many viewers disappointed.

senses.def: the last part of a word, such as -ed or -ing
examples: Past tense verbs usually take the ending -ed.

senses.def: very large in size or amount, or seeming never to stop
examples: I'm tired of endless meetings that achieve nothing.
The desert seemed to stretch into an endless horizon.

senses.def: to say publicly that you support a person, idea, or plan
examples: The newspaper endorsed her for governor.
The committee endorsed the proposal unanimously.

senses.def: to say in an advertisement that you use and like a product
examples: Famous athletes are paid millions to endorse sneakers.

senses.def: a public statement of support for a person, idea, or plan
examples: The senator won the endorsement of the largest teachers' union.
The plan received a strong endorsement from economists.

senses.def: a deal in which a well-known person promotes a product for money
examples: The tennis star earns more from endorsements than from prize money.

senses.def: to experience and deal with something painful or unpleasant for a long time
examples: The refugees endured weeks of hunger and cold.
She had to endure years of criticism before her work was accepted.

senses.def: to continue to exist for a long time (formal)
examples: Their friendship endured for over sixty years.

senses.def: a person who hates or opposes someone and tries to harm them
examples: He made a lot of enemies during his time as mayor.
The two families have been bitter enemies for generations.

senses.def: a country or army that you are fighting in a war
examples: The soldiers were captured behind enemy lines.

note: Opposite: friend, ally. "Your own worst enemy" = someone who causes their own problems.

senses.def: the physical and mental strength and enthusiasm you need to be active
examples: I don't have the energy to cook tonight.
Kids have so much energy in the morning.

senses.def: power from electricity, fuel, the sun, etc. used to run machines and heat buildings
examples: The country gets most of its energy from wind and solar power.
Energy prices rose sharply last winter.

senses.def: to make sure that people obey a law or rule
examples: Police are now strictly enforcing the speed limit near schools.
The rule is rarely enforced.

senses.def: to make something happen or force a situation to exist
examples: You can't enforce discipline by shouting at people.

senses.def: the act of making people obey a law or rule
examples: Stricter enforcement of traffic laws has reduced accidents.
Local law enforcement officers arrived within minutes.

note: In American English "law enforcement" often means the police and similar agencies (kolluk kuvvetleri).

senses.def: to attract and keep someone's interest or attention
examples: A good teacher knows how to engage a room full of teenagers.
The museum uses games to engage young visitors.

senses.def: to take part in an activity or become involved with someone (engage in / with)
examples: Students who engage in sports tend to do better at school.
The company needs to engage more with its customers.

senses.def: to employ someone for a particular job (formal)
examples: They engaged a lawyer to handle the sale of the house.

senses.def: having formally agreed to marry someone
examples: They got engaged last summer and plan to marry in June.
She's engaged to a doctor from Chicago.

senses.def: busy with or actively involved in something
examples: Students learn more when they are actively engaged in the lesson.

note: "Engaged to" (not "with") someone. In British English a phone line can be "engaged"; Americans say "busy".

senses.def: an agreement to marry someone, or the period before the wedding
examples: They announced their engagement at a family dinner.
He gave her an antique engagement ring.

senses.def: the act of being involved with or interested in something
examples: The new app increased user engagement by 30 percent.

senses.def: an arrangement to do something or meet someone, especially officially
examples: The minister had to cancel several speaking engagements.

senses.def: interesting or pleasant in a way that attracts and holds your attention
examples: She's an engaging speaker who keeps the audience laughing.
The book is an engaging account of life on a farm.

senses.def: the part of a vehicle or machine that produces power to make it move
examples: The car's engine wouldn't start on the cold morning.
One of the plane's engines caught fire shortly after takeoff.

senses.def: a vehicle that pulls a train
examples: The old steam engine pulled six passenger cars.

note: "Search engine" = arama motoru. "Motor" is used for smaller electric machines; cars have engines.

senses.def: a person whose job is designing and building machines, structures, systems, or software
examples: She works as a software engineer at a startup in Austin.
Civil engineers inspected the bridge after the earthquake.

senses.def: a person who drives a train or repairs and controls engines
examples: The train's engineer hit the brakes when he saw the car on the tracks.

senses.def: to design and build something, or to arrange something cleverly or secretly
examples: The crops have been genetically engineered to resist pests.
Critics say the crisis was engineered for political gain.

note: In American English the driver of a train is also called an "engineer".

senses.def: the work or study of using science to design and build machines, structures, and systems
examples: He has a degree in mechanical engineering from Purdue.
The bridge is a remarkable piece of engineering.

senses.def: to improve the quality, value, or strength of something
examples: A fresh coat of paint can enhance the value of your home.
The new lighting enhances the colors of the paintings.

note: Used for making good things better (enhance a reputation), not for repairing something bad.

senses.def: to get pleasure from something
examples: I really enjoy cooking for friends on the weekend.
Did you enjoy the concert last night?

senses.def: to have something good, such as a right or advantage (formal)
examples: The region enjoys a mild climate all year round.

note: Enjoy needs an object or reflexive: "enjoy yourself" (NOT "I enjoyed" alone). Followed by -ing: enjoy swimming.

senses.def: giving pleasure
examples: We had a very enjoyable evening at the lake.
The hike was long but surprisingly enjoyable.

senses.def: extremely large in size, amount, or degree
examples: They live in an enormous house with seven bedrooms.
The project was an enormous success.

note: "Enormity" usually means the great seriousness of something bad, not just large size.

senses.def: as much or as many as you need or want
examples: We don't have enough chairs for everyone.
Is there enough time to grab a coffee?

senses.def: to the necessary degree (placed after an adjective, adverb, or verb)
examples: He isn't old enough to drive.
You're not studying hard enough.

senses.def: a sufficient amount, or as much as you can accept
examples: I've had enough of your excuses.
Thanks, that's enough for me.

note: Word order trap: enough + noun (enough money), but adjective + enough (big enough), never "enough big".

senses.def: to ask someone for information (formal)
examples: Several customers called to enquire about the delay.
I'm writing to enquire whether the position is still open.

note: Mainly British spelling. American English almost always uses "inquire".

senses.def: a question you ask in order to get information
examples: We received hundreds of enquiries about the job.

senses.def: an official investigation into the cause of something
examples: The government has ordered an enquiry into the hospital deaths.

note: Mainly British spelling; Americans write "inquiry" (pronounced /ˈɪŋkwəri/ or /ɪnˈkwaɪəri/).

senses.def: to improve the quality of something, often by adding something to it
examples: Traveling abroad really enriched my life.
The cereal is enriched with iron and vitamins.

senses.def: to make someone richer, often unfairly
examples: Critics say the deal only enriched a few insiders.

senses.def: to officially join a course, school, or program, or to arrange for someone to join
examples: She enrolled in a night class to learn Spanish.
More than 2,000 students are enrolled at the college.

note: American spelling: enroll, enrollment; British: enrol, enrolment. Americans say "enroll in" a course.

senses.def: to happen after something or as a result of it (formal)
examples: The referee made a bad call, and a fight ensued.
In the ensuing chaos, several people were injured.

note: Formal. Usually intransitive and often in the form "the ensuing + noun".

senses.tr: sağlamak, garanti etmek, güvence altına almak
senses.def: to make certain that something happens or is true
examples: Please ensure that all windows are closed before you leave.
The new rules ensure equal pay for equal work.

note: Don't confuse with "insure" (sigortalamak) and "assure" (birine güvence vermek: assure someone that...).

senses.def: to come or go into a place
examples: Everyone stood up when the judge entered the room.
Thieves entered the house through a back window.

senses.def: to type or write information into a computer or form
examples: Enter your password and click "Log in".

senses.def: to take part in a competition, or to begin a job, period, or activity
examples: She entered the race at the last minute.
The war has entered its third year.

note: No preposition after enter for places: enter the room (NOT enter to/into the room). But "enter into" an agreement or discussion.

senses.def: a company or business
examples: The program offers loans to small and medium-sized enterprises.
The software is designed for large enterprises.

senses.def: a large or difficult project, especially a new one
examples: Building the railroad was a huge and risky enterprise.

senses.def: the ability to think of new projects and the energy to make them succeed
examples: The town's revival owes a lot to local enterprise.

senses.def: to interest or amuse people in order to give them pleasure
examples: A clown was hired to entertain the kids at the party.
The show aims to entertain as well as educate.

senses.def: to invite people to your home and give them food and drink
examples: They love to entertain, so their house is always full of guests.

senses.tr: (fikir, ihtimal) aklından geçirmek, göz önünde bulundurmak
senses.def: to consider an idea or possibility (formal)
examples: I never entertained the idea of quitting.

senses.def: enjoyable and interesting to watch, read, or listen to
examples: The movie is silly but very entertaining.
He's an entertaining storyteller who always makes us laugh.

senses.def: movies, music, shows, games, etc. that people enjoy, or the business that produces them
examples: There's live entertainment at the hotel every Friday night.
She works in the entertainment industry in Los Angeles.

senses.def: a strong feeling of excitement and interest in something
examples: The new coach brought energy and enthusiasm to the team.
She talked about her trip with great enthusiasm.

senses.def: a person who is very interested in an activity or subject and spends a lot of time on it
examples: The museum is popular with railroad enthusiasts.
He's a keen fitness enthusiast who runs every morning.

note: Informal American alternatives: "buff" (a history buff), "junkie", "nut".

senses.def: feeling or showing a lot of excitement and interest
examples: The kids were very enthusiastic about the camping trip.
The band got an enthusiastic welcome from the crowd.

note: Use "enthusiastic about" (NOT for/on).

senses.def: including every part, person, or thing; whole
examples: I spent the entire weekend cleaning the garage.
The entire town came out to watch the parade.

note: Used before a noun, usually with the/my/an: the entire team. "In its entirety" = as a whole.

senses.def: completely; in every way
examples: The meal was made entirely from local ingredients.
I'm not entirely sure what she meant.

note: "Not entirely" is a polite way to say "partly not": I'm not entirely convinced.

senses.def: to give someone the right to have or do something
examples: Full-time staff are entitled to four weeks of paid vacation.
This ticket entitles you to a free drink.

senses.def: to give a title to a book, movie, etc.
examples: Her first novel was entitled "The Long Road Home".

note: Mostly passive: be entitled to (something / do something). "Entitled" as an adjective can also mean spoiled, believing you deserve special treatment.

senses.def: something that exists separately and has its own identity, such as an organization
examples: After the merger, the two banks became a single entity.
The company operates as a separate legal entity.

note: Formal and academic; common in law and business.

senses.def: a door, gate, or passage that you use to enter a place
examples: Meet me at the main entrance of the museum.
The building has a separate entrance for deliveries.

senses.def: the right to go into a place or join a group; the act of coming into a room or onto a stage
examples: She passed the entrance exam for law school.
The actor made a dramatic entrance in the second act.

note: Opposite: exit. "Entrance exam" = giriş sınavı.

senses.def: a person who starts and runs businesses, especially when this involves financial risk
examples: The young entrepreneur launched her first company at 22.
The city offers grants to help local entrepreneurs.

note: Tricky spelling from French: entre-pre-neur.

senses.def: the act of going into a place, or the right to go in
examples: The thieves gained entry through an open window.
He was refused entry to the country because his visa had expired.

senses.def: a separate item in a diary, list, dictionary, or database
examples: The dictionary has over 50,000 entries.
Her last diary entry was dated June 3.

senses.def: something you submit in a competition
examples: The winning entry will be published in the magazine.

note: "Entry-level" = for beginners, with no experience needed (giriş seviyesi).

senses.def: a flat paper cover that you put a letter or card in before sending it
examples: She sealed the envelope and put a stamp on it.
The check arrived in a brown envelope.

note: "Push the envelope" = to go beyond normal limits. Don't confuse with the verb "envelop" /ɪnˈveləp/ (sarmak, kuşatmak).

senses.def: the natural world of land, water, air, plants, and animals
examples: Plastic waste is causing serious damage to the environment.
We need to protect the environment for future generations.

senses.def: the conditions and surroundings that affect how people live or work
examples: Children need a safe and loving environment to grow up in.
It's a fast-paced work environment.

note: In the "nature" sense it takes "the": damage the environment. Note the spelling: enviro-n-ment.

senses.def: connected with the natural world and its protection, or with surrounding conditions
examples: The new airport could have a serious environmental impact.
She joined an environmental group that cleans up local rivers.

note: "Environmentally friendly" = çevre dostu.

senses.def: a large number of cases of a disease in one community at the same time
examples: A flu epidemic closed schools across the state.
Health officials warned of a cholera epidemic after the floods.

senses.def: a sudden, fast increase in something bad
examples: Doctors are worried about the obesity epidemic among children.

note: Epidemic = in one area or country; pandemic = across the world.

senses.def: one part of a TV or radio series, or a podcast
examples: I stayed up late to watch the final episode of the season.
New episodes come out every Tuesday.

senses.def: a single event or short period that is important or unusual
examples: It was an embarrassing episode that he'd rather forget.
She had another episode of severe depression last year.

senses.def: the same in size, number, value, or rights as something or someone else
examples: Cut the cake into eight equal pieces.
Women and men should get equal pay for the same job.

senses.def: a person or thing with the same ability, rank, or rights as another
examples: She treats her employees as equals.
As a pianist, he had no equal.

senses.def: to be the same in amount or value as something, or to be as good as something
examples: Two plus three equals five.
Her time equaled the world record.

note: American spelling: equaled, equaling (British: equalled). "Be equal to a task" = be able to do it.

senses.def: the state of having the same rights, status, and opportunities as others
examples: The movement fought for racial equality in the 1960s.
Gender equality in the workplace is still a long way off.

senses.def: to the same degree or amount
examples: Both candidates are equally qualified for the job.
The prize money will be shared equally among the winners.

senses.def: used to add a second point that is as important as the first
examples: Exercise is important; equally, you need enough sleep.

note: Avoid "equally as": say "equally important" or "just as important".

senses.def: to think that one thing is the same as or closely linked to another
examples: Many people equate success with making a lot of money.
You can't equate criticism with disloyalty.

senses.def: to be equal to something in amount or value (equate to)
examples: The pay rise equates to about $50 a week.

note: Pattern: equate A with B. The idea is often criticized: "don't equate X with Y".

senses.def: a mathematical statement showing that two amounts are equal, such as 2x + 3 = 7
examples: The students had to solve five equations in ten minutes.
Einstein's famous equation links energy and mass.

senses.def: a situation in which several things must be considered together
examples: When you add children to the equation, moving abroad gets complicated.

collocations: the other side of the equation

senses.def: to provide someone or something with the tools or things needed for a purpose
examples: All police cars are equipped with cameras.
The gym is fully equipped with modern machines.

senses.def: to give someone the skills or knowledge they need
examples: The course equips students to work in the tech industry.

note: The p doubles: equipped, equipping.

senses.def: the tools, machines, or other things needed for a particular activity
examples: The hospital needs new medical equipment.
We rented all our camping equipment from a local store.

note: Uncountable: NOT "equipments" or "an equipment". Say "a piece of equipment".

senses.def: equal in value, amount, meaning, or importance
examples: The fine is equivalent to a month's salary.
Is there an equivalent word in Turkish?

senses.def: something that has the same value, purpose, or meaning as something else
examples: A tablespoon is the equivalent of three teaspoons.
He drank the equivalent of ten cups of coffee.

note: "Equivalent to" (adjective) vs. "the equivalent of" (noun).

senses.def: a period of history with particular features or events
examples: The fall of the Berlin Wall marked the end of an era.
We live in the era of social media.

note: "Usher in a new era" = to start a new period.

senses.def: to build something or put something in an upright position (formal)
examples: The town erected a statue in honor of the fallen soldiers.
Police erected barriers along the parade route.

senses.def: standing or sitting straight up
examples: The soldier stood erect as the flag was raised.

note: Formal; in everyday speech use "put up" or "build".

senses.def: to gradually wear away rock, soil, etc. by wind, water, or ice, or to be worn away
examples: The waves have eroded the cliffs over thousands of years.
Without trees, the soil quickly erodes.

senses.def: to gradually weaken or destroy something such as trust, power, or value
examples: The scandal has eroded public trust in the police.
Inflation is eroding people's savings.

senses.def: a mistake, especially one that causes problems or affects a result
examples: The crash was caused by human error.
There's an error in the second paragraph of your report.

note: More formal than "mistake". "Make an error" (NOT do an error). "Trial and error" = deneme yanılma.

senses.def: when a volcano erupts, it suddenly throws out fire, rocks, smoke, and lava
examples: The volcano erupted for the first time in 40 years.

senses.def: to start suddenly and violently or loudly
examples: Fighting erupted between rival gangs downtown.
The crowd erupted in cheers when the goal was scored.

senses.def: to become or make something worse, more serious, or more intense
examples: The argument quickly escalated into a fistfight.
Both sides are trying not to escalate the conflict.

senses.def: to rise rapidly in amount or cost
examples: Healthcare costs continue to escalate.

note: "Escalate an issue" in workplaces means to pass a problem to a higher manager.

senses.def: to get away from a place where you are kept against your will or from danger
examples: Two prisoners escaped from the jail overnight.
The family escaped the fire through a window.

senses.tr: (kötü bir şeyden) kurtulmak, yakayı sıyırmak; gözden kaçmak
senses.def: to avoid something bad, or to not be noticed or remembered
examples: The driver escaped serious injury.
Her name escapes me right now.

senses.def: the act of escaping, or something that helps you forget daily life
examples: The prisoner's escape made national news.
For me, reading is an escape from stress.

note: "A narrow escape" = kıl payı kurtuluş. "His name escapes me" = I can't remember it.

senses.def: more than usual or more than others; particularly
examples: I love fruit, especially strawberries.
Driving is dangerous here, especially at night.

senses.def: for a particular purpose or person
examples: I made this cake especially for you.

note: Position: usually right before the word it highlights (especially at night). "Specially" is mainly used for purpose: specially designed.

senses.def: a short piece of writing on a subject, especially one written by a student
examples: The professor asked us to write a 2,000-word essay on the Civil War.
Her college application essay was about her grandmother.

note: In US universities, students often say "paper" instead of essay.

senses.def: the most important quality of something that makes it what it is
examples: The essence of good teaching is listening to students.
In essence, the plan is to cut costs by 20 percent.

senses.def: a strong liquid taken from a plant and used for its flavor or smell
examples: Add a few drops of vanilla essence to the batter.

note: "Time is of the essence" = time is extremely important; we must hurry. Americans usually say "vanilla extract".

senses.def: completely necessary or extremely important
examples: Water is essential for life.
It's essential that you arrive on time for the exam.

senses.def: basic and central to the nature of something
examples: The essential difference between the two plans is cost.

senses.def: something that is necessary (usually plural)
examples: We only packed the essentials: water, food, and a map.

senses.def: when you consider the basic or most important nature of something
examples: The two phones are essentially the same, except for the color.
Essentially, he's a kind person who makes bad choices.

senses.def: to start an organization, system, or relationship that is meant to last
examples: The university was established in 1891.
The two countries established diplomatic relations last year.

senses.def: to discover or prove that something is true
examples: Investigators are trying to establish the cause of the fire.
Police have established that he was at home that night.

senses.def: to make people accept you or something in a particular role
examples: She quickly established herself as one of the best lawyers in the city.

senses.def: an organization, business, or institution such as a hotel, store, or restaurant
examples: The restaurant is a family-owned establishment that opened in 1952.
Smoking is banned in all public establishments.

senses.def: the act of starting or creating something
examples: The establishment of the national park protected the forest.

senses.def: the people and institutions that have power and influence in a society (the Establishment)
examples: The candidate ran as an outsider against the political establishment.

senses.def: a large area of land in the country, usually with a big house, owned by one person or family
examples: The family's estate includes a vineyard and a lake.

senses.def: all the money and property a person owns, especially what is left when they die
examples: She left her entire estate to an animal charity.
His estate was worth over $5 million.

senses.def: (British) an area of land with many houses or factories of the same type
examples: He grew up on a housing estate outside Manchester.

note: "Real estate" (gayrimenkul) is very common in American English. A British "estate agent" is an American "real estate agent" or "realtor".

senses.def: a guess of the size, value, or cost of something, made without exact figures
examples: By some estimates, the storm caused $2 billion in damage.
At a rough estimate, about 500 people attended.

senses.def: a written statement of how much a job will probably cost
examples: Get at least three estimates before hiring a contractor.

senses.def: to guess the size, cost, or value of something without calculating it exactly
examples: Experts estimate that the bridge will cost $40 million.
The crowd was estimated at 10,000.

note: Pronunciation differs: noun /ˈestɪmət/, verb /ˈestɪmeɪt/.

senses.def: lasting or existing forever, without an end
examples: Many religions promise eternal life after death.
They swore eternal love to each other.

senses.def: seeming to continue forever, often in an annoying way
examples: I'm tired of their eternal arguments about money.

note: "I'll be eternally grateful" is a common way to give strong thanks.

senses.def: a set of moral principles or beliefs that guide how someone behaves
examples: She has a strong work ethic and never misses a deadline.
The company tries to follow an ethic of honesty with its customers.

senses.def: moral rules for a group or profession, or the study of right and wrong (ethics)
examples: The senator was investigated for violating ethics rules.
She teaches medical ethics at the university.

note: Singular "ethic" mostly appears in "work ethic"; otherwise use "ethics" (takes a plural or singular verb).

senses.def: connected with beliefs about what is morally right and wrong
examples: Cloning animals raises serious ethical questions.
Doctors face ethical dilemmas every day.

senses.def: morally correct or acceptable
examples: Is it ethical to test cosmetics on animals?
She only buys from ethical clothing brands.

senses.def: connected with a group of people who share a culture, language, or origin
examples: The city is home to many ethnic groups.
Ethnic minorities are still underrepresented in Congress.

senses.def: typical of a culture different from the main one in a country
examples: The neighborhood is full of ethnic restaurants.

note: "Ethnic food" is becoming less used; many prefer naming the cuisine (Thai, Ethiopian).

senses.def: the unit of money used in many countries of the European Union
examples: The hotel costs 120 euros a night.
The dollar rose against the euro this week.

note: In Turkish it's "avro" or "euro"; in English the plural is "euros".

senses.def: to move people from a dangerous place to a safer one, or to leave a dangerous place
examples: Thousands of residents were evacuated before the hurricane hit.
Staff had to evacuate the building after a gas leak.

senses.def: to judge the quality, value, or importance of something after careful thought
examples: Teachers evaluate students on homework, tests, and participation.
We need to evaluate the risks before we invest.

senses.def: the act of judging how good, useful, or successful something is
examples: Every employee gets a performance evaluation once a year.
The program is still under evaluation.

senses.def: used to emphasize something surprising or unexpected
examples: He didn't even say goodbye.
Even my grandma has an Instagram account now.

senses.def: used with comparatives to make them stronger
examples: The second movie was even better than the first.

senses.def: flat and smooth, or equal and balanced
examples: Spread the paint in an even layer.
The score was even at halftime.

senses.def: able to be divided exactly by two
examples: Two, four, and six are even numbers.

note: Opposite of an even number is an odd number (tek sayı). "Break even" = neither gain nor lose money.

senses.def: the part of the day between late afternoon and bedtime
examples: We usually go for a walk in the evening.
Are you free on Thursday evening?

senses.def: an event or social occasion that happens in the evening
examples: The school is hosting a music evening for parents.

note: Use "in the evening" but "on Monday evening". "Good evening" is a greeting; say "good night" when leaving.

senses.def: something that happens, especially something important or unusual
examples: The book describes the events leading up to the war.
Her death was a tragic event for the whole town.

senses.def: a planned public or social occasion, or one race or competition in a sports program
examples: The charity event raised over $50,000.
She won gold in the 200-meter event.

note: "In the event of" (formal) = if something happens: In the event of fire, use the stairs.

senses.def: happening at the end of a long process or period of time
examples: The team lost in the semifinals to the eventual champions.
The eventual cost of the project was double the estimate.

note: False friend: "eventual" does NOT mean "possible" (olası). It means what finally happens.

senses.def: at the end of a period of time or a series of events, often after delays
examples: After three hours of waiting, we eventually got a table.
You'll eventually get used to the cold winters here.

note: False friend: NOT "possibly" (Turkish "eventüel/olası"). "Eventually" = in the end.

senses.def: at any time, used mainly in questions, negatives, and comparisons
examples: Have you ever been to New York?
This is the best pizza I've ever had.

senses.def: used to mean "always" or "increasingly" in certain phrases
examples: Prices keep rising ever higher.
They lived happily ever after.

note: Use with present perfect for life experience: Have you ever...? "Hardly ever" = almost never.

senses.def: used with a singular noun to mean all members of a group, one by one
examples: Every student must bring a photo ID to the exam.
I walk the dog every morning before work.

senses.def: used to show how often something happens, at regular intervals
examples: The bus comes every ten minutes.
Take one pill every four hours.

note: Takes a singular verb: Every student has a laptop. "Every other day" = gün aşırı.

senses.def: every person; all the people in a group
examples: Everybody at the party was dancing.
Does everybody have a copy of the agenda?

note: Same as "everyone" but slightly more informal. Singular verb: Everybody is here.

senses.def: happening or used every day; ordinary and normal
examples: Smartphones have become part of everyday life.
These are simple recipes made with everyday ingredients.

note: One word = adjective (everyday clothes). Two words = adverb phrase: I go running every day.

senses.def: every person; all people
examples: Everyone in my family loves soccer.
Thanks, everyone, for coming tonight.

note: Singular verb, but "they/their" is normal: Everyone has their own opinion. "Every one" (two words) = each single item.

senses.def: all things, or all the things in a situation
examples: The fire destroyed everything they owned.
Is everything OK? You look upset.

senses.def: the most important thing to someone
examples: My kids are everything to me.

senses.def: in, to, or at every place
examples: I've looked everywhere for my keys.
There were tourists everywhere in the old city.

senses.def: facts, signs, or objects that show that something is true
examples: There is strong evidence that smoking causes cancer.
Police found no evidence of a break-in.

senses.def: information or objects used in a court of law to prove something
examples: The knife was presented as evidence at the trial.

note: Uncountable: NOT "an evidence" or "evidences". Say "a piece of evidence".

senses.def: clear and easily seen or understood
examples: It was evident from her face that she was upset.
His love for the game is evident in every match he plays.

senses.def: morally very bad and enjoying harming others
examples: The movie is about an evil queen who poisons her stepdaughter.
Slavery was an evil system.

senses.def: great moral wrong, or a force that causes bad things to happen
examples: The story is about the battle between good and evil.
Poverty and disease are the great evils of our time.

note: "The lesser of two evils" = ehven-i şer. Very strong word; for small wrongs use "bad" or "mean".

senses.def: to bring a feeling, memory, or image into your mind
examples: The smell of baking bread evokes memories of my childhood.
The photos evoke the hardships of life during the Depression.

senses.def: the slow development of plants and animals over millions of years as they adapt
examples: Darwin's theory of evolution changed biology forever.
Fossils give us clues about human evolution.

senses.def: the gradual development of something into a different or more advanced form
examples: The museum shows the evolution of the car over 100 years.

senses.def: connected with evolution or with slow, steady development and change
examples: Birds are the evolutionary descendants of dinosaurs.
The new phone is an evolutionary step rather than a revolution.

senses.def: to develop gradually, especially from a simple to a more complex form
examples: The company has evolved from a small shop into a global brand.
Language is always evolving.

senses.def: (of plants and animals) to change over many generations through evolution
examples: Whales evolved from land mammals.

senses.def: correct in every detail; completely accurate
examples: Do you know the exact time the train leaves?
I can't remember his exact words.

senses.def: to demand and get something, often by force (formal)
examples: The gang exacted revenge on the man who betrayed them.

note: "To be exact" adds precision: It took two hours, 140 minutes to be exact.

senses.def: used to say that something is correct in every detail
examples: The meeting starts at exactly 9 a.m.
That's exactly what I wanted to say.

senses.def: used as a reply to show strong agreement
examples: "So we need more time?" "Exactly."

note: "Not exactly" is often ironic or polite: He's not exactly friendly (= he's quite unfriendly).

senses.def: to make something seem bigger, better, or worse than it really is
examples: He always exaggerates how much money he makes.
The risks have been greatly exaggerated by the media.

note: Spelling trap: double g, single r. Opposite: understate, play down.

senses.def: a formal test of knowledge or skill, especially at school or college
examples: I have a chemistry exam on Monday morning.
She passed all her final exams with high grades.

senses.def: a medical check of part of the body
examples: You should get an eye exam every two years.

note: "Take an exam" = sınava girmek (NOT "give an exam", which is what the teacher does). Americans also say "test" for smaller exams.

senses.def: a careful look at or study of something or someone
examples: A closer examination of the data revealed several errors.
The doctor performed a full physical examination.

senses.def: a formal test of knowledge or skill (formal)
examples: Candidates must pass a written examination to become lawyers.

note: "Exam" is the everyday word for a test; "examination" is formal.

senses.def: to look at or consider something carefully in order to learn about it
examples: The study examines the effects of social media on teenagers.
Experts examined the painting to see if it was a fake.

senses.def: to look at someone's body carefully to check their health
examples: The doctor examined my knee and ordered an X-ray.

senses.def: something that shows what a group of things is like or supports a general idea
examples: Can you give me an example of a renewable energy source?
Many cities, for example Paris and Amsterdam, have banned old cars.

senses.def: a person or behavior that others should copy
examples: Parents should set a good example for their children.

note: "Make an example of someone" = punish someone to warn others.

senses.def: to be greater than a particular number, amount, or limit
examples: The cost of repairs could exceed $10,000.
He was fined for exceeding the speed limit.

senses.def: to be better than what was expected or hoped
examples: The results exceeded all our expectations.

senses.def: the quality of being extremely good
examples: The hospital is known for its excellence in cancer care.
She received an award for excellence in teaching.

senses.def: extremely good
examples: The food at that restaurant is excellent.
She speaks excellent English.

note: Already very strong, so don't use "very": NOT "very excellent".

senses.def: not including; apart from
examples: The store is open every day except Sunday.
Everyone was invited except me.

senses.def: used before a fact that makes a statement not completely true
examples: I'd love to come, except I have to work that night.
The twins look identical except that one has longer hair.

note: Don't confuse with "accept" (kabul etmek), which sounds similar.

senses.def: a person or thing that does not follow a general rule or is not included
examples: All the rooms were small, with the exception of the kitchen.
Most of the songs were great, and this one was no exception.

note: "Take exception to" (formal) = to be offended by something.

senses.def: unusually good
examples: She's an exceptional student who finished college at nineteen.
The wine from that year was of exceptional quality.

senses.def: very unusual and not likely to happen often
examples: Refunds are only given in exceptional circumstances.

senses.def: an amount that is more than necessary, usual, or acceptable
examples: An excess of salt in your diet can raise blood pressure.
He was known for his life of excess.

senses.def: more than is needed or allowed
examples: The airline charged me for excess baggage.
Cut off any excess fat before cooking the meat.

note: "In excess of" (formal) = more than: in excess of $1 million.

senses.def: much more than is reasonable or necessary
examples: The officers were accused of using excessive force.
Excessive drinking can damage your liver.

senses.def: the act of giving something and receiving something in return
examples: He offered to fix their computer in exchange for dinner.
The two countries agreed to a prisoner exchange.

senses.def: a short conversation or argument, or a visit where people from two countries swap places
examples: There was a heated exchange between the two senators.
She spent a year in Japan as an exchange student.

senses.def: to give something and receive something of the same kind in return
examples: We exchanged phone numbers before saying goodbye.
Can I exchange this shirt for a smaller size?

note: "Exchange rate" = döviz kuru. "Exchange glances/words/gifts" = to give to each other.

senses.def: feeling very happy and enthusiastic, especially about something that will happen
examples: The kids are so excited about going to Disneyland.
I'm really excited to start my new job next week.

note: The person feels excited; the thing is exciting. Use "excited about" (NOT "excited for" in formal writing, though it's common in speech).

senses.def: something you want to achieve and are working toward
examples: My goal is to run a marathon before I turn forty.
The company set an ambitious goal of cutting emissions in half.

senses.def: a point scored by getting the ball into the net, or the net and frame itself
examples: She scored the winning goal in the final minute.
The ball hit the post and bounced away from the goal.

senses.def: (usually God) the being that many religions believe created and rules the universe
examples: Many people pray to God for strength in hard times.
Do you believe in God?

senses.def: one of many spirits that some religions worship as having power over nature or people
examples: Zeus was the king of the Greek gods.
The ancient Egyptians had a god of the sun.

note: Capitalize God for the one god of a religion. "Oh my God" is common but some people find it offensive; "oh my gosh" is softer.

senses.def: a valuable yellow metal used for jewelry, coins, and as an investment
examples: The ring is made of solid gold.
Investors often buy gold when the stock market is falling.

senses.def: a gold medal, given to the winner of a competition
examples: She won gold in the 100-meter sprint.

senses.def: made of gold, or having its bright yellow color
examples: He wore a gold watch to the wedding.
The invitation was printed in gold letters.

note: "Gold" is used for things made of the metal or its color; "golden" is more poetic or figurative (a golden opportunity).

senses.def: made of gold, or bright yellow like gold
examples: The king wore a golden crown.
The field was full of golden wheat.

senses.def: very good, special, or likely to bring success
examples: This is a golden opportunity to expand into new markets.
The 1960s were the golden age of television.

senses.def: a game in which players hit a small ball into a series of holes using clubs, in as few shots as possible
examples: My father plays golf every Saturday morning.
They discussed the deal over a round of golf.

senses.def: of high quality, pleasant, or at an acceptable standard
examples: This is a really good restaurant.
We had good weather for the whole trip.

senses.def: able to do something well
examples: She's very good at math.
He is good with children.

senses.def: helpful or healthy for someone, or morally right and kind
examples: Fresh vegetables are good for you.
It was good of you to help us move.

senses.def: behavior that is morally right, or something that benefits someone
examples: The battle between good and evil is an old theme in stories.
Complaining won't do any good.

note: Irregular: good – better – best. Use "well" as the adverb (She sings well). "For good" means "forever".

senses.def: what you say when you or another person is leaving
examples: Goodbye, everyone. See you on Monday!

senses.def: the act of saying goodbye when someone leaves
examples: We said our goodbyes at the airport.
It was a tearful goodbye after twenty years together.

note: "Wave/kiss goodbye to something" can also mean you will lose it: You can kiss your deposit goodbye.

senses.def: the quality of being kind, honest, and morally good
examples: She believes in the basic goodness of people.

senses.def: used to express surprise, often in phrases like "my goodness"
examples: My goodness, look how tall you've grown!
Thank goodness you're safe.

senses.def: things that are made to be sold, or things that someone owns and can move
examples: The store sells sporting goods and outdoor gear.
Tariffs raised the price of imported goods.

note: Always plural; there is no "a good" in this sense. Use "a product" or "an item" for one.

senses.def: very beautiful or attractive, or very pleasant
examples: You look gorgeous in that dress.
We had gorgeous weather for the beach party.

note: Informal and enthusiastic. Common for people, places, food, and weather.

senses.def: to officially control a country, state, or its people and make its laws
examples: The country was governed by the military for ten years.
The party has governed the state since 2010.

senses.def: to control or strongly influence how something happens or is done
